title: Why Wordle Works, According to Desmos Lesson Developers
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Meyer asks what math class can learn from Wordle and polls the Desmos lesson designers. Their answers become design principles: a simple question that reveals its constraints quickly, expected failure, feedback that attaches meaning to incorrect thinking, multiple routes to the same answer, a shareable representation of learning, and social learning via one puzzle a day. He ends with a challenge to lesson designers to build these features into their own work. The piece is a curriculum-design argument grounded in practitioners' observations rather than research.
points: A good learning task has a core question that is easy to explain and hard to fully answer.
Normalizing failure works when being wrong early is built into the task and carries little consequence.
Effective feedback tells learners what is right about wrong answers and leaves actionable next steps.
Tasks that allow multiple routes to the answer invite creativity and conversation.
Scarcity and a shareable, spoiler-free artifact (the emoji grid) turn individual learning into a social experience.
quotes: The games and stories that have endured longest in our imagination all have a question at their core that is very easy to explain and very hard to fully answer.

Effective feedback attaches meaning to thinking—even and especially incorrect thinking. Expert teachers know that feedback messages like "you're right" and "you're wrong" are less effective than feedback that invites the student who got it right to deepen their thinking and helps the student who got it wrong to see the value in their incorrect answers.
Wordle rewards every thought you bring to it with something new to think about.

The feedback is specific to my response and shows me which parts of my response are useful in the solution and which parts of my response are not useful. The feedback leaves me with actionable next steps.
The same is true with Wordle. Whenever my colleagues trade their answers, they all have the same mystery word, but no two people reached it through the same route of words.
I think one of the most genius moves design-wise was to make it only a single game per day. By doing this, a game that could become addictive and isolating instead brings people together.
Can you offer feedback that goes beyond "right" and "wrong," that helps learners identify everything right about their wrong answers?
